title: Lina and the Careful Fast
markdown:
The Whispering Woods buzzed like a thousand tiny bees getting ready for a picnic. The annual Jungle Jamboree was about to begin: the obstacle challenge where every creature, from beetle to giraffe, could test strength and cleverness. Lina, a leopard cub with spots bright as polished acorns and eyes full of go, wanted the Golden Acorn. She had practised with every whisker, every muscle, every bit of her speedy spirit. She could already feel the trophy’s cool weight in her paws.

“Who is ready to fly, flutter, and bound?” hooted Bethan the owl, master of ceremonies, from the oldest oak. Her feathers looked as ancient as the tree. She knew how to get a forest excited without knocking anyone off a branch.

Lina’s tail twitched like a happy question mark. Beside her stood Gus the goose, a picture of calm. He stretched his long neck, pearly feathers ruffling. Gus was not built for sprinting or mountains. He had the best eyes in the woods. He had watched the practice rounds from dawn to dusk, noticing the slightest slip.

“I am more than ready, Gus,” Lina chirped. “I’m going to be the fastest. Zoom. Shooting star. Think of the Acorn.”

Bethan dropped a leaf. That was the start. The first teams dashed off in a blur of fur and feathers. Vine Tango: twisty hanging vines that wanted to dance you into a knot. Lina’s team took it in a streak, Squeaky calling left and Pip rolling under a loop like a polished pebble. Slippery Slope: extra-slick moss. Lina’s claws found the dull patches her mother would have chosen. Wobbly Wonder: rocking logs. They crossed in a rhythm, almost a joke. Lina’s paws tingled. She was so, so ready. The Golden Acorn felt one obstacle closer, cool in her mind.

Then the path led to the Rope Bridge: thick vines strung high over a brook that sparkled like dropped diamonds. Every year teams rushed it, paws thudding, noise a jumble. Every year someone stumbled, lost a seed bag needed later, or knotted themselves into the ropes. It was the part everyone talked about, and not kindly. Seed bags hung at each team’s belt for the planting relay after the mud. Lose one and you ran the last stretch for show.

Gus tilted his head. “Look, Lina. The cheetahs. Lightning at the start. One lost a footing on a loose knot and had to climb back. The monkeys swung too hard and made a heap of tails. Minutes they can’t get back.”

Lina watched her eagerness dim a little, like sun behind a quick cloud. Gus was right. The magnificent blur was now huffing, trying to catch those who had already passed. One cheetah’s pride had become a scramble, belly to rope, while a beetle team they had laughed at earlier picked a slow neat line and went by. The monkeys, usually graceful, were a funny time-consuming knot, tails arguing about whose idea the swing had been. The faster they tried to be on that swaying bridge, the more time they spent correcting themselves. Lina’s own legs still wanted to run. She made them wait and watch, which was a new sport and a harder one.

“They want to be fast,” Gus said. “The bridge wants a different kind of fast. A careful fast. A thoughtful fast.”

Lina’s brow furrowed. She remembered her mother on the mossy river rocks. One paw, then the next. Steady and sure. Never rush the rocks.

The words clicked against Gus’s phrase like two stones making a spark. “We don’t race it like a runaway vine,” she said. “We stay on it.”

When their turn came she did not sprint. A hare team snorted past the waiting line and hit the first plank already leaning. Lina looked back. Gus nodded. She stepped onto the first rope and tested it. It gave a little, then held. Then the next. Then the next. Each paw a decision. Squeaky the squirrel, nimble and quick-witted, kept the seed bag tight against his chest. Pip the pangolin, scales like tiny shields, put his weight where Lina had put hers, a shining echo. They did not rush. They held on. They moved as a unit. Once the bridge swayed hard and Lina waited, counting three of Gus’s blinks, before the next step. Gus called, “Be steady, little ones.”

Teams who had zoomed the bridge were already far ahead, and already in the mud pit that came after, sucking at paws, spending the minutes they thought they had earned. A cheetah’s seed bag bobbed away downstream like a small brown boat. Lina’s team reached the end without a wobble, without losing a seed. The mud, when they came to it, was only mud. They chose the edges, where roots made a kind of path, and went through with their bags still singing with seeds.

The last stretch was the planting relay: seeds into prepared hollows along the finish meadow. Because their bags were full, they planted as they ran, which looked slower and was not. They crossed the finish with paws and tiny claws together. The Golden Acorn caught the dappled light. Lina did not make a speech. She set one careful paw on the trophy’s base, the same way she had set it on the first rope, and grinned at Gus, who honked as if that were the whole joke and the whole prize. Squeaky counted seeds under his breath, a happy maths. Pip shone.

Bethan, from the oak, blinked once, slowly, which for an owl is applause. The brook under the empty bridge kept sparkling. The next team, watching, put a foot down as if the rope might listen.
characters: Lina (a leopard cub), Gus (a goose with sharp eyes), Bethan (an old owl)
